candidate.blueprint_locator: Reduction of Risk Potential: interpret laboratory findings and trends, recognize risk related to fluid volume/perfusion changes, and integrate diagnostic data with client condition.
candidate.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — BUN interpretation in volume depletion
candidate.educational_objective: Interpret elevated BUN as a nonspecific finding that can support prerenal azotemia in a volume-depleted client when integrated with clinical status and other renal data rather than treating it as diagnostic by itself.

options.A: The elevation can support a prerenal process related to water depletion or reduced renal perfusion when interpreted with the clinical picture and other renal data.
options.B: The elevation specifically proves postrenal urinary obstruction regardless of the client's volume status or other findings.
options.C: The elevation demonstrates improved glomerular filtration because BUN rises as renal clearance becomes more efficient.
options.D: The elevation is unrelated to hydration or renal perfusion and should not influence assessment of a volume-depleted client.

candidate.rationale: Current Mayo Clinic Laboratories information states that increased BUN can result from prerenal causes such as water depletion from decreased intake or excessive loss and cardiac decompensation/reduced renal perfusion, but BUN can also increase from renal and postrenal causes. It is therefore interpreted with the clinical picture and commonly alongside creatinine rather than as a stand-alone diagnosis. In this volume-depleted client, A is the appropriate interpretation. B overstates specificity for obstruction, C reverses the relationship to clearance, and D incorrectly dismisses the relevance of hydration and perfusion.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Elevated BUN in a clinically volume-depleted client can support a prerenal process from water depletion or reduced perfusion, but BUN is nonspecific and requires contextual interpretation.
candidate.source_locator: Clinical Information: increased BUN may be due to prerenal causes including cardiac decompensation and water depletion from decreased intake/excessive loss; renal and postrenal causes are also listed. BUN is frequently requested with serum creatinine to aid differential diagnosis of prerenal, renal, and postrenal hyperuremia.

candidate.stem: A client with vomiting and poor intake is clinically volume depleted and has an elevated blood urea nitrogen (BUN). Which interpretation is most appropriate?
